newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia short-term rates ease on overseas funds.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia short-term rates ease on overseas funds.

text.p: Inflow of overseas funds through swaps pulled down domestic short-term rates despite a 500 million ringgit Bank Negara bill issue payment, dealers said on Wednesday.
They said one-week rate fell to 7.40/50 percent against 8.10/20, two-week fell to 7.40/50 percent from 7.90/8.00 and three-week was unchanged at 7.50/60.
One-month to three-month money was down at 7.40/50 percent against 7.50/55 and six-month was unchanged at 7.50/55 percent.
"Banks are borrowing in the swaps market and lending locally," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank.
He said the rise of interbank rates over the last two weeks had created several arbitrage opportunities, which were being exploited at the moment.
Dealers said on Wednesday morning one-week money in the swaps market was at 6.9 percent, which still gave a difference of 50-60 basis points over the domestic interest rates.
One dealer said the effective yield on overnight money was around 7.5 percent in the swaps market against around 8.7 at close on Tuesday.
"These differences are more than sufficient to attract large funds from the overseas markets," the dealer said.
Most dealers said there was no reason for interest rates to come off despite the temporary fall caused by swap funds.
"The market sentiment is still for firm rates because overall the situation is still very tight," a dealer with a large Malaysian bank said.
In addition, swap opportunities were narrowing down.
Reflecting the change, interest rate futures reversed a week-long trend and were up across the board on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange.
The three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) June contract was up two points at 92.64, or an implied yield of 7.36 percent.
September was up three at 92.65, or 7.35 percent, and December up three at 92.58, or 7.42 percent.
